books.section: Topic 4.9 The Development of an American Culture, B. European Romanticism and American Culture

stimulus.text: Thomas Cole, The Course of Empire: Destruction, 1836, is the fourth of five paintings tracing an imaginary city's rise and fall. A burning classical city fills the canvas: crowds flee across a bridge, a great statue topples from its pedestal at right, and smoke darkens the sky. Cole signed and dated the pedestal "1836."
stimulus.source_note: Painting: Thomas Cole, The Course of Empire: Destruction, 1836 (New-York Historical Society). Public domain; image viewed before writing. Description records only what the painting visibly shows.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The fact that Cole painted an imaginary classical city, rather than an American scene, best shows which of the following?

options.text: He had never seen an American landscape
options.misconception: The city is not American, so it is easy to think Cole had never painted America.

options.text: American painters were forbidden to paint American places
options.misconception: No American city appears, so it is easy to imagine a rule against painting one.

options.text: The past as a mirror for their own republic
He wanted his paintings sold in Europe only
options.misconception: Classical scenes sold well in Europe, so it is easy to think Europe was his only market.

rationales.A: Cole painted American wilderness all his life; The Oxbow alone proves he knew it well.
rationales.B: No such rule existed; Cole's other paintings are full of American scenes.
rationales.C: An imaginary Rome lets every American viewer ask whether their own republic could fall the same way.
rationales.D: The series was painted for an American patron in New York, not for sale abroad.
rationales.general:
1. Ask why an American painter would paint Rome. Not to show Rome, but to show America something.
2. Ask what Rome lends him. A finished story of rise and fall, ready to hold up as a mirror.
Background: Cole's series warned that empires, like republics, could fall, and Americans were its audience.
Remember: when an artist borrows a distant past, ask what present fear it is dressed to carry.

figures.caption: Thomas Cole, The Course of Empire: Destruction, 1836. A burning classical city, crowds fleeing, a statue toppling.
figures.alt: Thomas Cole's 1836 painting of a burning classical city: crowds flee across a bridge while a huge statue topples from its pedestal at right and smoke fills the sky
